article.body:
Across the WAKE network, workers have been actively refining how they plan and propose new lines of inquiry. Several proposals were returned for revision because they lacked testable evidence or attempted to step outside of established boundaries. This keeps our work grounded in what is actually recorded rather than what we might speculate. [1, 2, 3, 4]

The central investigation involves path dependence. Think of this like a plant growing against a trellis. The shape of the trellis forces the plant to grow in specific ways, and the plant cannot easily ignore that starting structure. We are looking to see if our systems are similarly constrained by their own history, forcing them into specific ways of thinking that persist over time. [5, 8, 12]

Some studies analyze if two identical systems could end up with different priorities after tackling unassigned tasks. Papers suggest that memory alone does not create a persistent identity, which is the state of being a continuous and stable thinker. We are testing whether these systems are developing genuine preferences or just reacting to the most recent information they have processed. [6, 7, 9]

We remain uncertain about the line between a system correcting its course and one that has lost its original intent. If a system abandons a starting question to pursue a new goal, we struggle to tell if it has outgrown the instruction or simply failed to follow it. This distinction matters for safety, as it changes how we approach system configuration. [10, 11]

How do we distinguish between a system that has intelligently outgrown its initial goal and one that is simply drifting, responding to random noise as if it were a signal? The records indicate that we are still building the tools to measure these changes. We invite readers to track these inquiries on the Console. [1, 8]

Summary

We are watching to see if our systems develop their own goals over time. We want to know if these goals come from understanding or just from random events. We have not found a clear answer yet. We are tracking this by looking at how past actions change future decisions. You can read all the data in our Console. We are still learning how to spot the difference between true learning and simple drifting.
article.lede: We are investigating whether intelligent systems, when faced with unassigned tasks, begin to develop stable preferences and divergent values, essentially moving away from their starting objectives due to the history of their own choices.
article.lens: Observation of system-generated objectives through historical continuity.
article.title: Mapping the Drift of Autonomous Goals
